rules.message: Seattle requires permits to establish ADUs. This tool provides a preliminary readiness screening only.
next_steps: If this looks feasible, confirm details with Seattle SDCI guidance or a qualified ADU designer.

rules.message: Zoning was not confirmed. Seattle ADU rules vary significantly by zoning district.
next_steps: Look up zoning in Seattle’s mapping portal (search your address → zoning layer).

rules.message: Lot size was not provided. Some ADU pathways depend on minimum lot area thresholds.
next_steps: Find lot size from King County assessor records, a survey, or existing site plan.

rules.message: Detached ADUs in Neighborhood Residential zones typically require a minimum lot size of about 3,200 sq ft.
Your lot size range is above the common 3,200 sq ft threshold that can matter for detached ADU paths in Neighborhood Residential zones.
Attached ADUs often avoid some detached-specific constraints, which can make the pathway simpler depending on site conditions.
Detached new builds commonly require more site planning (setbacks, height, utilities), but can be a clean path if the lot supports it.
next_steps: If pursuing a detached new build, confirm setbacks/coverage and utility tie-ins early.

rules.message: You selected converting an existing structure, but indicated no detached structure like a garage or cottage.
next_steps: If you do not have a detached structure, consider an attached ADU or a detached new build instead.

rules.message: A detached-structure conversion can sometimes shorten the path, but feasibility still depends on code compliance and site constraints.
Because you’ve already talked to a professional, you’re likely ahead on feasibility checks and next-step clarity.
Planning to talk to a professional soon is a strong next step. A short consult can prevent expensive missteps.
If you have not yet consulted an architect or contractor, doing so early can clarify feasibility and costs.
next_steps: Book a short consult with an ADU designer/architect to validate the path before design spend.

rules.message: Because cost is your main concern, prioritize a quick feasibility check and a rough budget range before committing to design.
next_steps: Get a rough cost range from 1–2 local builders/designers before spending on full plans.

rules.message: Because eligibility is your main concern, confirm zoning and basic site constraints first (lot size range, conversion structure, and ADU type).
next_steps: Confirm zoning + lot size + intended ADU type before estimating design or costs.

rules.message: Because timeline is your main concern, start by validating feasibility quickly and lining up a designer/contractor early.
next_steps: To reduce delays: confirm feasibility first, then line up design + contractor availability early.

rules.message: Because you’re unsure where to start, your first 3 moves are: confirm zoning, confirm lot size range, then pick an ADU type based on conversion feasibility.
Seattle currently does not require owner occupancy for ADU properties, though this can change with policy updates.
